name: Rolipram
lead: Rolipram is a selective phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4) inhibitor. By slowing the breakdown of the signalling molecule cAMP, it affects inflammation and brain signalling, which is why it has been used widely as a research tool and was developed as an antidepressant.[1][2] In recovery-minded circles it is mentioned for its anti-inflammatory and memory-related effects, which proponents connect to training recovery, mood and sleep, and through them to how a person looks.

Schering AG developed rolipram as a possible antidepressant; trials found a narrow therapeutic window because doses high enough to be effective brought gastrointestinal side effects, and development ended.[1] It remains an investigational compound and the prototype for later PDE4 inhibitors such as cilomilast.[3][3]

chain: Proponents link this to recovery and mood
angle.text: Rolipram is discussed as an anti-inflammatory, pro-cAMP compound that people hope will support recovery and cognition, indirectly supporting training consistency and appearance.

paras: PDE4 is an enzyme family that breaks down cyclic AMP; PDE4B in particular is described as a regulator of brain signalling relevant to cognition and neuroinflammation.[2] PDE4 is the dominant phosphodiesterase in immune cells such as neutrophils, eosinophils, mast cells and macrophages, where its inhibition reduces activation.[4] Rolipram is the reference compound used to study this mechanism.[3]
Reported oral bioavailability is about 75%, with liver metabolism by several CYP enzymes and an elimination half-life of about 3 hours.[1]

Rolipram was discovered and developed by Schering AG as an antidepressant candidate. Its narrow therapeutic window ended its clinical development, but it became a prototype for other companies' PDE4 programs.[1] Second-generation PDE4 inhibitors such as cilomilast were designed to retain rolipram's activity with an improved profile.[3]

Rolipram was tested in depression in the 1980s and early 1990s: a phase II study of its antidepressant effect, and randomized comparisons with imipramine and amitriptyline in major depression.[5][6][7] A phase II trial of rolipram in multiple sclerosis was registered in 2001, and imaging studies have used radiolabelled rolipram to measure PDE4 in the brain.[8][9]

In animals, rolipram has facilitated long-lasting long-term potentiation and memory, improved synaptic and cognitive function in an Alzheimer mouse model, and, with Schwann cells, promoted axon growth after spinal cord injury.[10][11][12] These are laboratory findings. Chemotherapy-related cognitive problems are among conditions where PDE4 inhibitors such as rolipram have been proposed for study.[13]
The gastrointestinal side effects that limited the dose are the main reported adverse effect.[1]

card.summary: A PDE4 inhibitor studied for inflammation and cognition, discussed by some for recovery, mood and memory that support training and appearance.
card.note: Investigational only; gastrointestinal side effects limited dosing in trials.

quick.overview:
Rolipram is a PDE4 inhibitor, a compound that raises cAMP signalling. It was developed by Schering as an antidepressant and is now mostly a research tool.

People interested in recovery follow it for its anti-inflammatory and memory-related effects, which they connect to training, mood and, indirectly, appearance.
quick.mechanism: It blocks PDE4, the enzyme that breaks down cAMP, which affects immune-cell activation and brain signalling involved in memory.
quick.risks: Gastrointestinal side effects limited the doses that could be used, and development as a drug ended. It is investigational and not an approved medicine.
